title: Human Perceptions of Fairness in Algorithmic Decision Making
abstract: As algorithms are increasingly used to make important decisions that affect human lives, ranging from social benefit assignment to predicting risk of criminal recidivism, concerns have been raised about the fairness of algorithmic decision making. Most prior works on algorithmic fairness normatively prescribe how fair decisions ought to be made. In contrast, here, we descriptively survey users for how they perceive and reason about fairness in algorithmic decision making. A key contribution of this work is the framework we propose to understand why people perceive certain features as fair or unfair to be used in algorithms. Our framework identifies eight properties of features, such as relevance, volitionality and reliability, as latent considerations that inform people»s moral judgments about the fairness of feature use in decision-making algorithms. We validate our framework through a series of scenario-based surveys with 576 people. We find that, based on a person»s assessment of the eight latent properties of a feature in our exemplar scenario, we can accurately (> 85%) predict if the person will judge the use of the feature as fair. Our findings have important implications. At a high-level, we show that people»s unfairness concerns are multi-dimensional and argue that future studies need to address unfairness concerns beyond discrimination. At a low-level, we find considerable disagreements in people»s fairness judgments. We identify root causes of the disagreements, and note possible pathways to resolve them.

claims.text: A person's assessment of eight latent properties of a feature accurately predicts whether they will judge the feature's use in algorithmic decision making as fair with over 85% accuracy.
A majority of survey respondents judged five of the ten evaluated COMPAS features as unfair to use for predicting criminal recidivism risk.
Less than 3% of surveyed respondents reported using a feature consideration outside of the proposed eight latent properties when judging fairness.
Each of the eight proposed latent properties was relied upon by at least 15% of surveyed respondents as a consideration in their fairness judgments.

Disagreements in people's fairness judgments stem primarily from differences in how they estimate latent properties rather than differences in their moral reasoning mapping latent properties to fairness.
Evaluations of latent properties related to causality exhibit lower consensus among respondents than non-causal latent properties.

limitations.text: Prior works on algorithmic fairness largely focus on normative prescriptive definitions, assuming an unverified societal consensus on what constitutes fair decision making.
Survey responses rely on self-reported ratings which may introduce self-report biases.
Empirical evaluation was conducted within a single specific decision-making scenario (COMPAS criminal recidivism risk prediction for bail).
Amazon Mechanical Turk workers suffer from selection bias and are not demographically representative of the U.S. population.

future_work.text: Validate whether fairness prediction models based on self-reported inputs align with human fairness perceptions when people are placed in ecologically valid real-world interactions with decision-making algorithms.
Explore the extent to which the identified latent property fairness heuristic varies across different cultures and decision-making contexts.

methodologies.name: Scenario-Based Survey and Latent Property Predictive Modeling
methodologies.description: Evaluated user fairness perceptions and latent feature property ratings across 10 COMPAS risk assessment features using online surveys, followed by binary logistic regression modeling to map latent property ratings to fairness judgments.
conditions: Scenario context: Broward County bail release risk estimation
Randomized feature and property presentation orders
